paper_title: Reinforcing Diffusion Models by Instantaneous Trajectory Distribution Matching

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Forward diffusion reinforcement learning (RL)---enabling deterministic ODE sampling without trajectory backpropagation---has grown increasingly popular for efficiently aligning diffusion models. However, we reveal that existing methods essentially rely on signed reward-weighted regression (RWR), regressing the trainable policy velocity onto rollouts from a behavior distribution. Unbiased baseline subtraction implicitly assumes that the policy velocity equals the behavior marginal velocity---an idealized assumption violated under classifier-free guidance (CFG) rollouts, offline/off-policy updates, and imperfect online self-consistency. This behavior--policy mismatch breaks baseline invariance and injects baseline-induced gradient drift, destabilizing training. To resolve this issue, we propose Instantaneous Trajectory Distribution Matching (iTDM), taking the infinitesimal limit of Trajectory Distribution Matching toward a time-local reward-guided target via the posterior-score identity to yield a sample-level gradient anchored at the behavior velocity without learning an additional reward-tilted target score. Tracking this velocity with an online auxiliary denoiser guarantees exact baseline invariance at the auxiliary optimum, effectively suppressing baseline drift across both online and offline RL. Extensive experiments across compositional generation, text rendering, and preference alignment show that iTDM achieves state-of-the-art in-domain and out-of-domain performance across group-wise online/offline RL and pairwise offline RL. Notably, on the challenging GenEval2 benchmark, iTDM converges nearly 3\times faster than competing methods while scaling smoothly to 0.87 without collapse. Furthermore, iTDM scales effectively to the 5.6B FLUX.3 model, achieving better performance across both in-domain and unseen metrics. Code is available at https://github.com/Luo-Yihong/iTDM

Introduction Reinforcement learning (RL) has become cornerstone for post-training generative models, advancing large language models (Bai et al., 2022; DeepSeek-AI, 2025; Shao et al., 2024; Ziegler et al., 2019) and empowering diffusion and flow-matching models in compositional generation, text rendering, iTDM 2 Figure 2 Samples generated by iTDM on the 5.6B FLUX.3 Klein Base (Black Forest Labs, 2026), reinforced with HPSv3++ (Liu et al., 2026) in the guidance-free regime (CFG = 1.0). iTDM 3 Figure 3 Qualitative comparisons on human preference alignment (PickScore) with SD3.5-M. All models are trained and evaluated under CFG = 1.0. Compared with competing forward diffusion RL baselines, iTDM faithfully follows intricate prompt details while delivering sharper textures and superior aesthetic quality, avoiding blurry artifacts. and preference alignment (Black et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2025; Wallace et al., 2024; Xue et al., 2025b). Early online diffusion RL methods (Liu et al., 2025; Xue et al., 2025b) apply trajectory-level policy gradients via stochastic differential equation (SDE) samplers, sacrificing the efficiency and fidelity of deterministic ordinary differential equation (ODE) solvers while incurring heavy trajectorybackpropagation overhead. Consequently, forward diffusion RL (Luo et al., 2025d; Xue et al., 2025a; Zheng et al., 2025)which collects clean rollouts via deterministic ODE solvers and optimizes policies along the forward noising pathhas gained popularity for its training efficiency. In GRPO-style post-training (Shao et al., 2024), subtracting prompt-level baseline 𝑏(c) to form centered advantages (𝐴 = 𝑅 𝑏(c)) is essential for variance reduction and relative preference learning. However, we reveal that existing forward diffusion RL methods (Luo et al., 2025d; Xue et al., 2025a; Zheng et al., 2025) essentially rely on signed reward-weighted regression (RWR): the rollout sampler defines behavior distribution 𝑞0 with marginal velocity 𝑣𝑞(x𝑡, 𝑡), whereas RWR evaluates its denoising residual at the trainable policy velocity 𝑣𝜃(x𝑡, 𝑡). Unbiased baseline subtraction therefore implicitly rests on an idealized assumption: 𝑣𝜃 = 𝑣𝑞. Yet this assumption fails in practice under classifier-free guidance (CFG) rollouts, offline/off-policy updates, and imperfect online self-consistency, creating pervasive behaviorpolicy mismatch (𝑣𝜃 𝑣𝑞) with two severe side effects: (1) Baseline-induced gradient drift: non-zero residual mean (𝑣𝜃 𝑣𝑞 0) breaks baseline invariance and injects spurious drift proportional to 𝑏(c)(𝑣𝜃 𝑣𝑞), causing unanchored RWR to collapse and existing methods to stagnate or diverge under CFG-guided and offline RL; and (2) Coarse rollout-artifact fitting: RWRs inherent pull toward 𝑞𝑡 drives 𝑣𝜃 to fit few-step ODE discretization artifacts, degrading textures and out-of-domain fidelity (Figs. 3 and 5). We argue that these failures stem not from centered advantages, but from forcing distributional policy improvement into signed regression tied to the fragile behavior-policy consistency assumption (𝑣𝜃 = 𝑣𝑞). Based on this insight, an ideal forward diffusion RL method should tolerate the effects of behaviorpolicy mismatch without drifting toward coarse few-step rollouts. To this end, we propose Instantaneous Trajectory Distribution Matching (iTDM), principled distribution-matching framework for forward diffusion RL. Via the Gaussian posterior-score identity, iTDM converts the intractable target score into an exact sample-level RL gradient anchored at the behavior velocity 𝑣𝑞, without learning an additional reward-tilted target score. Theoretically, iTDM ensures exact baseline invariance even when 𝑣𝜃 𝑣𝑞. Practically, we track 𝑣𝑞 online with an auxiliary denoiser 𝑣𝜙, guaranteeing exact baseline invariance at the auxiliary optimum and effectively suppressing baseline drift. Offline RL and Diagnostic Analysis Group-Wise Frozen-Rollout RL. With 𝑞0 frozen to pretrained SD3.5-M (CFG = 4.5), using the initial velocity 𝑣𝜃0 as static proxy in offline AWM and NFT leaves persistent mismatch (𝑣𝜃0 𝑣𝑞; Fig. 8 and Tab. 4). Consequently, NFT collapses below the base model (0.52 vs. 0.63 GenEval; 0.53 vs. 0.59 OCR) and AWM diverges after peaking at 0.75 GenEval. Supported by its decoupled stationary policy (Lemma 2) and baseline invariance at the auxiliary optimum (Lemma 3), iTDM improves monotonically to 0.87 GenEval (+9% over DGPO), 0.92 OCR, and 22.26 PickScore while leading DrawBench generalization. iTDM 14 Figure 9 Pairwise offline RL (𝐺 = 2, CFG = 4.5) vs. Diffusion-DPO. Pairwise RL (𝐺 = 2) and Group Scaling. Unlike pairwise-only DPO (Wallace et al., 2024), iTDM supports arbitrary group sizes. Under identical pairwise rollouts (𝐺 = 2, Fig. 9), iTDM converges faster and outperforms DPO on all tasks (0.77 vs. 0.69 GenEval, 0.87 vs. 0.78 OCR, 22.11 vs. 21.87 PickScore) and all seven unseen metrics. Scaling to larger groups (Fig. 8 and Tab. 4) further boosts performance (0.77 0.87 GenEval, 0.87 0.92 OCR). Diagnostic Controls. Figs. 4 and 6 verify the crucial control: removing proximity anchors collapses on-policy RWR, confirming that NFT and AWM rely on heuristic anchors to damp baseline drift, whereas iTDM suppresses it via 𝑣𝜙 with better rewards and training stability. 5. Related Work Aligning diffusion and flow-matching models with human preferences or downstream rewards generally follows three paradigms: supervised fine-tuning on curated imageprompt pairs (Dai et al., 2023; Podell et al., 2023), explicit reward maximization via multi-step output backpropagation (Clark et al., 2023; Lee et al., 2023; Luo et al., 2025a,b; Prabhudesai et al., 2023), control/score matching (Domingo-Enrich et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2026; Psenka et al., 2023), or policy gradients (Black et al., 2023; Fan et al., 2023; Ren et al., 2024; Ye et al., 2024), and implicit preference learning such as Diffusion-DPO (Wallace et al., 2024), Diffusion-KTO (Li et al., 2024), and group-enumerated variants (Chen et al., 2025). Recently, Flow-GRPO (Liu et al., 2025) and DanceGRPO (Xue et al., 2025b) adapted GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) to visual generation, inspiring refinements in hybrid sampling, branching, scheduling, and video alignment (He et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025a,b, 2026; Liang et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026, 2025a,b). However, these trajectory-based methods remain tied to stochastic transition likelihoods and costly multi-step trajectory training. To enable fast deterministic ODE rollouts without trajectory backpropagation, recent forward diffusion RL methods optimize policies directly on independently re-noised endpoints. Beyond group-level preference optimization in DGPO (Luo et al., 2025d), DiffusionNFT (Zheng et al., 2025), AWM (Xue et al., 2025a), EPG/PEPG (Choi et al., 2026b), and RAM (Bergmeister et al., 2026) (alongside (Xu et al., 2026; Ye et al., 2025)) formulate velocity-space updates, which RVM (Choi et al., 2026a) unifies at the gradient level as reward-weighted velocity regression with anchor regularization. Yet, because these RWR-style losses evaluate the residual at 𝑣𝜃, under CFG rollouts, offline/off-policy updates, or imperfect online self-consistency (𝑣𝜃 𝑣𝑞), subtracting reward baseline violates baseline invariance and induces population gradient drift (Sec. 3.4). By taking the step-normalized infinitesimal limit of Trajectory Distribution Matching (Luo et al., 2025c), iTDM anchors the sample-level residual at the behavior velocity via lightweight auxiliary denoiser, guaranteeing exact baseline invariance and drift-free optimization at the auxiliary optimum to enable stable online and offline RL. iTDM 6. Conclusion 15 In this work, we revealed that existing forward diffusion RL methods essentially rely on signed RWR, whose implicit 𝑣𝜃 = 𝑣𝑞 assumption breaks down under behaviorpolicy mismatch to induce baseline gradient drift while pulling policies toward coarse few-step rollout artifacts. To resolve both issues, we introduced Instantaneous Trajectory Distribution Matching (iTDM), which takes the infinitesimal limit of TDM toward time-local reward-guided target via the posterior-score identity, yielding an exact sample-level RL gradient anchored at the behavior velocity without learning an additional reward-tilted target score. Paired with lightweight online auxiliary LoRA denoiser and reference regularization, iTDM guarantees exact baseline invariance at the auxiliary optimum, suppresses drift and artifact fitting, and unifies online and offline RL. Extensive experiments across SD3.5-M and the 5.6B FLUX.3 model demonstrate up to 3 faster convergence alongside state-of-the-art in-domain and out-of-domain performance across diverse tasks and post-training regimes.
